fetched_contents.text: Editorial: Registered reports on the role of representational competencies in multimedia learning and learning with multiple representations ---------------------------------------- External representations are information carriers that commonly manifest in various formats, such as text, graphs, or formulas, displayed, for example, in educational resources, such as textbooks or computer-based learning programs. The use of more than one external representation, i.e., the combination of various types of representations for conveying information related to a specific topic or concept, is called multimedia learning (mostly for text-picture combinations; Mayer and Fiorella, 2022) or learning with multiple external representations (Ainsworth, 2006). There is evidence suggesting that learning with multiple representations, rather than single representations, can foster learning (e.g., Lee et al., 2006; Eitel et al., 2013) and problem-solving (e.g., Lindner et al., 2017; Ott et al., 2018). The term representational competencies or competence refers to the ability to select, analyze, and utilize external representations to support claims, explain concepts, make predictions, and draw inferences. Representational competencies involve specific skills, such as transforming one representation into another, selecting appropriate representations, and understanding how different representations convey information in distinct ways (Kozma and Russell, 1997). Representational competencies have been found to be positively correlated with conceptual knowledge (Edelsbrunner et al., 2023). There are different assumptions about how representational competencies might affect learning processes related to multiple external representations. Learning with multiple representations can place high demands on learners, since they are required to handle complex, domain-specific representations (e.g., Stieff et al., 2011). It is assumed that a representation dilemma can occur when learners are offered representations that include essential information but fail to benefit from them due to their lack of representational competencies (Rau, 2017). Accordingly, one could perceive representational competence as a prerequisite for successful learning with multiple representations. However, there is also the assumption that representational competence and content or conceptual knowledge can be acquired simultaneously through appropriate instruction. Moreover, first evidence suggests that there may be gender differences in the strength of the relationship between representational competencies and conceptual knowledge, suggesting gender-specific interventions (Edelsbrunner et al., 2023). Despite some initial intriguing findings coming exclusively from Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math (STEM) subjects, research on the role of representational competencies for learning with external representations is still in its infancy. This Research Topic aims to bring together research that examines the interplay of representational competencies, associated skills and aptitudes, and learning with multiple representations. All articles are Registered Reports. The planned and pre-registered studies are published in this Volume 1 of the Research Topic as stage 1 papers. The corresponding stage 2 papers will be published in Volume 2 of the Research Topic upon their completion. Volume 1 includes four articles from various STEM disciplines. The stage 1 paper “Unraveling the relation between representational competence and conceptual knowledge across four samples from two different countries” by Edelsbrunner and Hofer intends to study the statistical relation of representational competence and conceptual knowledge in physics education. The authors aim to further investigate this relationship by re-analyzing data from a previous study that found a significant positive correlation between these two constructs in the context of vector-field representations and electromagnetism (Küchemann et al., 2021). The data, collected from 515 undergraduate students across two countries, will be used to examine whether the relationship between representational competence and conceptual knowledge varies across different sub-samples. The goal is to understand the generalizability of this relationship and to derive hypotheses for potential moderating factors that can be further examined in future research. Another paper that deals with physics education is the stage 1 paper by Hahn and Klein, titled “The impact of multiple representations on students' understanding of vector field concepts: implementation of simulations and sketching activities into lecture-based recitations in undergraduate physics.” The research aims to investigate the effectiveness of multi-representational learning tasks in enhancing students' understanding of vector calculus concepts in the context of electrodynamics. The developed tasks focus on the visual interpretation of vector field diagrams and incorporate different representational activities such as sketching and using interactive simulations. In their field study, the authors will compare the impact of these multi-representational tasks to traditional calculation-based tasks on university students' mathematical as well as conceptual understanding of vector calculus concepts and on their cognitive load. fetched_contents.text: REPRESENTATIONAL-COMPETENCY SUPPORT 1 Adaptive support for representational competencies during technology-based problem solving in chemistry Martina A. Rau, Miranda Zahn, Edward Misback, Tiffany Herder, & Judith Burstyn Journal of the Learning Sciences, Volume 30, Issue 2 (2021) Published online: 12 March 2021 https://www.tandfonline.com/action/authorSubmission?show=instructions&journalCode=hlns 20#peers REPRESENTATIONAL-COMPETENCY SUPPORT 2 Abstract Background. A key aspect of STEM learning is the use of visual representations for problem solving. To successfully use visuals, students need to make sense of how they show concepts and to fluently perceive domain-relevant information in them. Adding support for sense making and perceptual fluency to problem-solving activities enhances students' learning of content knowledge. However, students need different types of representational-competency supports, depending on their prior knowledge. This suggests that adaptively assigning students to sense-making and perceptual-fluency support might be more effective than assigning all students to the same sequence of these supports. Method. We tested this hypothesis in an experiment with 44 undergraduate students in a chemistry course. Students were randomly assigned to a ten-week sequence of problem- solving activities that either provided a fixed sequence of sense-making support and perceptual-fluency support or adaptively assigned these supports based on students' problem- solving interactions. Findings. Results show that adaptive representational-competency supports reduced students' confusion and mistakes during problem solving while increasing their learning of content knowledge. Contribution. Our study is the first to show that adaptive support for representational competencies can significantly enhance learning of content knowledge. Given the pervasiveness of visuals, our results may inform general STEM instruction. REPRESENTATIONAL-COMPETENCY SUPPORT 3 Keywords Multiple representations, representational competencies, sense-making competencies, perceptual fluency, chemistry REPRESENTATIONAL-COMPETENCY SUPPORT 4 Visual representations play a key role in problem-solving practices in science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) domains (Kozma, Chin, Russell, & Marx, 2000; Wertsch & Kazak, 2011). When scientists study a phenomenon of interest, they typically visually represent the phenomenon, so that they can use the visual representation to reflect on the nature of the phenomenon. During this reflection process, they may gather new data and revise their visual representation to reflect new discoveries. Indeed, observational studies of expert scientists in chemistry and other STEM domains shows that their problem-solving practices critically rely on such representation-reflection iterations (Fan, 2015; Kozma & Russell, 2005a; Latour, 1986). Therefore, an important part of STEM instruction is for students to learn to use visual representations to solve disciplinary problems (Gilbert, 2005; NRC, 2006; Rau, 2017). The goal of this article is to investigate ways to support students in this learning process. Most STEM disciplines use established visual representations that have evolved as part of problem-solving practices that required reasoning about visuo-spatial concepts (Gilbert, 2005; NRC, 2006). Because different visual representations can illustrate different aspects of these phenomena, STEM instruction typically involves multiple visual representations (Ainsworth, 2006; Kozma et al., 2000; Rau, 2017). For example, chemists typically use a variety of visual representations (see Figure 1) to illustrate concepts related to atomic structure and bonding. --- Insert Figure 1 about here --- REPRESENTATIONAL-COMPETENCY SUPPORT 5 While multiple visual representations can help students learn, they also pose an educational dilemma (Ainsworth, 2006; NRC, 2006; Rau, Aleven, & Rummel, 2015). Instructional activities often present problems that engage students in reflection about domain-relevant concepts. Students are to explore these concepts by manipulating visual representations, which mimics common representation-reflection iterations that are part of disciplinary practices. However, because both the concepts and the representations are novel to students, students have to learn about how the visual representations show information about the concepts while also learning about the concepts from the visual representations. This conundrum is known as the representation dilemma (Dreher & Kuntze, 2015; Rau, 2017). To overcome the representation dilemma, students need representational competencies, which allow them to understand how various visual representations show information about different aspects of complex concepts in the given domain (Gilbert, 2005, 2008; NRC, 2006). Indeed, representational competencies have been shown to enhance students' learning of domain knowledge in math (Cheng, 1999; Noss, Healy, & Hoyles, 1997), physics (Klein, Viiri, Mozaffari, Dengel, & Kuhn, 2018; Larkin & Simon, 1987), biology (Treagust & Tsui, 2013), and chemistry (Kozma et al., 2000; Stieff, Hegarty, & Deslongchamps, 2011). Branch 3: educational implications and practical application

The evidence base suggests that representational competencies are not just a vague “ability to use representations,” but a set of specific skills that can be targeted in teaching and learning. Across the sources, the key educational implication is that students need instruction that helps them select, analyze, and use external representations effectively, especially when multiple representations are involved. The source material emphasizes that representational competencies support learning by enabling students to understand how representations show information, transform one representation into another, and perceive domain-relevant information in visualizations [N1-F1], [N3-F2]. This means the categories are not just abstract labels; they point to concrete instructional goals.

## How the categories inform teaching and learning with multiple representations

The most directly useful framing for teaching comes from the editorial and the math education article. The editorial defines representational competencies broadly as the ability to select, analyze, and utilize external representations to support claims, explain concepts, make predictions, and draw inferences [N1-F1]. It also notes that representational competencies involve specific skills such as transforming one representation into another, selecting appropriate representations, and understanding how different representations convey information in distinct ways [N1-F1]. This is a strong educational signal: teaching should not merely present multiple representations; it should explicitly help students recognize which representations are relevant, how they relate to each other, and how to use them for meaning-making.

The math education source reinforces this by framing representational competence as the ability to use representations meaningfully to understand and communicate mathematical ideas and solve problems [N3-F3]. It then lists four illustrative abilities: conveying an idea in various forms, knowing when and why a representation is appropriate, translating between and within modes of representations, and using representations flexibly to solve problems [N3-F3]. These are practical teaching targets because they suggest a progression from basic representation use to higher-order reasoning with multiple representations.

## Example activities or tasks that target each category

The evidence supports a variety of task types that can be aligned with the competencies, though the sources do not provide a fully explicit three-category taxonomy in the fetch material. Still, the closest explicit framing comes from the editorial and from the science/math education sources.

1. **Selecting appropriate representations**  
   Example: In a math class, students are asked to solve a word problem about multiplication by representing it in two different ways, one of which must be a visual or physical representation [N3-F3]. The teacher records student ideas such as connecting cubes, drawing a picture, grid paper, arrays, and tape diagrams [N3-F3]. This task directly targets the competence of selecting and using representations meaningfully [N3-F3].

2. **Translating between representations**  
   Example: Students are asked to convert a symbolic equation into a graph or a table, or vice versa, and then explain what each representation shows [N1-F1]. The editorial explicitly notes that representational competencies involve transforming one representation into another [N1-F1]. A science class using diagrams, graphs, and tables to represent the same phenomenon also fits this category [N4-R3], [N4-R5].

3. **Sense-making from representations**  
   Example: In a chemistry or physics problem-solving context, students are asked to interpret a diagram or graph, identify what information it shows, and explain how it relates to the underlying concept [N1-F1]. The source material also notes that students need to make sense of how visual representations show concepts and fluently perceive domain-relevant information in them [N3-F2]. In the physics education context, MERs are defined as learning from two or more external representations simultaneously, including diagrams, formulas, and data tables [N2-R3].

## Limitations or caveats for applying the categories

The evidence suggests several important caveats. First, the sources emphasize that representational competencies are not a single skill but a set of interrelated abilities, and the editorial explicitly states that there are different assumptions about how these competencies affect learning processes [N1-F1]. That means the categories should not be treated as rigid, fixed labels; they are best understood as a constellation of competencies that can overlap or vary in emphasis depending on the domain and task.

Second, the sources note that learning with multiple representations can place high demands on learners because they must handle complex, domain-specific representations [N1-F1]. The editorial also warns that a representation dilemma can occur when learners are offered representations that include essential information but fail to benefit from them due to lack of representational competencies [N1-F1]. So, simply exposing students to multiple representations is not sufficient; instruction must also support sense-making and perceptual fluency [N3-F2].

Third, the sources indicate that the strength of the relationship between representational competencies and conceptual knowledge may vary across subgroups, including by gender [N1-F1]. This means that the categories should be used with caution in educational design, and interventions should be adapted to the learner’s prior knowledge and context [N3-F2].

Overall, the practical takeaway is that representational competencies should be taught as a layered set of skills: selection, translation, and sense-making. Activities should vary across modes of representation, require students to move between representations, and explicitly connect representations to conceptual understanding. But they should also be implemented thoughtfully, with attention to learners’ readiness and the complexity of the domain [N1-F1], [N3-F2], [N3-F3].

## The three named categories

It also notes that representational competencies involve specific skills such as transforming one representation into another, selecting appropriate representations, and understanding how different representations convey information in distinct ways [N1-F1]. This is the most direct named three-category split in the provided evidence. The math education source does not provide the same explicit three-category taxonomy, but it does describe related abilities that map closely to those categories: conveying an idea in various forms, knowing when and why a representation is appropriate, translating between representations, and using representations flexibly to solve problems [N3-F3]. These can be interpreted as overlapping but distinguishable aspects of representational competence.

## How each category is defined in the source

1. **Linking between representations**  
   The earthquake-cycle source defines this as part of the three competencies necessary for earthquake cycle investigations [N6-R3]. In the broader literature, the editorial implies linking through the ability to transform one representation into another and to understand how different representations convey information in distinct ways [N1-F1]. The math education source also emphasizes translating between and within modes of representations [N3-F3]. This category is best understood as the ability to connect different representations and recognize relationships among them.

2. **Sensemaking from representations**  
   The earthquake-cycle source also identifies sensemaking as one of the three competencies [N6-R3]. The editorial similarly notes that representational competencies involve understanding how representations show information and making sense of visualizations [N1-F1]. The math education source describes the ability to convey a mathematical idea in various forms, knowing when and why a representation is appropriate, and using representations flexibly to solve problems [N3-F3]. Together, these sources define sensemaking as the ability to interpret a representation, extract meaning from it, and use it to reason about the underlying concept.

3. **Conceptualization or interpretation**  
   The earthquake-cycle source uses “conceptualization” as the third competency [N6-R3]. The editorial and math education sources support this as the broader goal of representational competence: using representations meaningfully to understand and communicate ideas [N1-F1], [N3-F3]. The math education source explicitly states that representational competence includes being able to use representations flexibly to solve problems and knowing when and why a representation is appropriate [N3-F3]. This category is best interpreted as the ability to interpret representations in terms of the underlying concept and use them to build conceptual understanding.

## Whether the source treats them as distinct or overlapping constructs

The sources generally treat the competencies as related but not identical constructs, and they sometimes overlap. The editorial describes representational competencies as a set of skills that include selecting, analyzing, and utilizing representations, as well as transforming one representation into another and understanding how representations convey information differently [N1-F1]. This suggests that the competencies are distinct in form, but the source also emphasizes that they are part of an interdependent skill set [N1-F1].

The math education source similarly describes several related abilities that can be grouped into overlapping but different aspects of representational competence [N3-F3]. It treats the competencies as a set of proficiency dimensions rather than as completely separate, mutually exclusive categories. The earthquake-cycle source explicitly names three competencies—linking, sensemaking, conceptualization—but the wording implies that these are distinct enough to be listed separately [N6-R3]. However, the evidence does not provide a detailed taxonomy of how these categories relate to one another in the source material, so the distinction should be understood as approximate rather than fully formal.

In summary, the best-supported three-category framework in the provided evidence is **linking**, **sensemaking**, and **conceptualization** [N6-R3], while the editorial and math education sources support the broader idea of representational competencies as distinct but overlapping skills centered on selection, transformation, interpretation, and flexible use of representations [N1-F1], [N3-F3]. The sources do not give a fully formal taxonomy, so the categories should be treated as a practical, domain-oriented classification rather than a rigidly defined ontology.

The clearest distinction comes from the editorial, the science/math education sources, and the earthquake-cycle source. ## What each category represents in terms of meaning, method, and interpretation

1. **Linking between representations**  
   Meaning: Linking is about recognizing relationships among different representations and moving between them.  
   Method: It involves transforming one representation into another, translating between modes, and connecting representations in a way that preserves meaning [N1-F1], [N3-F3].  
   Interpretation: The learner must see how one representation corresponds to or differs from another, and how they jointly convey the same concept [N1-F1].  
   The editorial explicitly states that representational competencies involve transforming one representation into another, selecting appropriate representations, and understanding how different representations convey information in distinct ways [N1-F1]. The math education source similarly emphasizes translating between and within modes of representations [N3-F3].

2. **Sensemaking from representations**  
   Meaning: Sensemaking is about interpreting a representation to extract meaning and understand the underlying concept.  
   Method: It involves making sense of how a visual representation shows information, fluently perceiving domain-relevant information in it, and using the representation to reason about the concept [N1-F1], [N3-F2].  
   Interpretation: The learner must not only read the representation but also interpret what it shows about the phenomenon or problem [N1-F1].  
   The editorial and the math education source both emphasize that students need to make sense of representations and use them meaningfully [N1-F1], [N3-F3]. The earthquake-cycle source also treats sensemaking as one of the three competencies needed for investigations [N6-R3].

3. **Conceptualization or interpretation**  
   Meaning: Conceptualization is about building an understanding of the underlying concept from the representation.  
   Method: It involves using representations flexibly to solve problems, knowing when and why a representation is appropriate, and interpreting representations in terms of the concept they represent [N3-F3].  
   Interpretation: The learner must connect the representation to the conceptual structure it illustrates and use it to form a coherent understanding [N3-F3].  
   The math education source states that representational competence includes using representations flexibly to solve problems and knowing when and why a representation is appropriate [N3-F3]. The sources show that external representations differ in the type of work they require and the skills they demand.

The earthquake-cycle source’s three competencies—linking, sensemaking, conceptualization—capture this well: linking is the method of connecting representations, sensemaking is the interpretation of each representation, and conceptualization is the overall understanding built from them [N6-R3].

## When one category is more relevant than another

The sources indicate that the relevance of each category depends on the task, the learner’s prior knowledge, and the nature of the representation.  

- **Linking is more relevant when students need to move between representations or reconcile differences among them**. This is especially important in mathematics, where students are asked to represent a problem in two different ways, and in science, where multiple external representations are used simultaneously [N3-F3], [N2-R3].  
- **Sensemaking is more relevant when students need to interpret a single representation and extract meaning from it**. The editorial notes that representational competencies involve making sense of how visual representations show concepts [N1-F1]. The math education source also emphasizes knowing when and why a representation is appropriate [N3-F3].  
- **Conceptualization is more relevant when students need to connect representations to a broader conceptual framework**. The math education source describes representational competence as the ability to use representations flexibly to solve problems and communicate mathematical ideas [N3-F3]. The editorial also suggests that representational competencies are prerequisite for successful learning with multiple representations [N1-F1].

The sources also suggest that these categories are not always mutually exclusive. For example, a single task can require linking representations while also making sense of them and conceptualizing the underlying idea. The editorial and the earthquake-cycle source both indicate that the competencies are interrelated and may be used together [N1-F1], [N6-R3]. However, the evidence also implies that they should not be treated as interchangeable; each has a distinct role in learning with multiple representations [N1-F1], [N3-F2], [N3-F3].

Overall, the best-supported distinction is that linking is about connecting representations, sensemaking is about interpreting them, and conceptualization is about using them to build understanding. The sources treat them as related but distinct competencies, with each becoming more relevant depending on the task and the learner’s stage of development [N1-F1], [N3-F3], [N6-R3].
